articles.title: More details emerge about FlyDubai co-pilot who tried to crash plane
articles.summary: Questions about the motive of the co-pilot who tried to crash a packed flight from Dubai to Israel continue to swirl.
articles.body:
Days after a FlyDubai co-pilot made a violent attempt to crash the passenger aircraft and was subdued by passengers and other crew members, questions about his motive continued to swirl.

The flight Wednesday from Dubai to Tel Aviv was approaching Israel when the co-pilot allegedly stabbed the flight captain and attempted to crash the aircraft, Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said. The captain was able to fight off the co-pilot long enough to unlock the cockpit door. Passengers then overpowered the co-pilot, and two off-duty pilots who were on the flight managed to gain control of the aircraft and make an emergency landing in Tabuk, Saudi Arabia.

There were 174 people on board the plane . No passengers were seriously injured in the incident. The pilot sustained stab wounds in the attack. Saudi authorities said two crew members were hospitalized with unspecified injuries, and the co-pilot remained in custody on Thursday.

The co-pilot of the flight has not yet been publicly identified, although multiple sources familiar with the investigation told CBS News on Friday that his name is Hamam al Hamami.

Al Hamami worked for a short time for Oman Air, where he entered new pilot training. Surveillance by the Omani government discovered that he was visiting radical websites, the sources said. Oman Air then transferred him to an office job.

One of the sources said the pilot resigned from his job at Oman Air after being placed on desk duty. He left the airline around 2024.

At one point, sources said, al Hamami posted a video of El Al Israeli Airlines planes in Dubai with a photo at the end of the clip showing Ayman al-Zawahiri, a well-known al Qaeda leader who was killed in a U.S. drone strike in 2022.

Al Hamami moved to Dubai, and FlyDubai hired him without vetting him with the Omani government, the sources told CBS News.

Al Hamami is an Omani citizen but was not born in Oman, the sources said. He lived most of his life outside Oman, according to the sources, who disclosed that his mother is Syrian and his father is Omani.

The Omani government has not publicly confirmed his nationality.

The sources said it is possible he had dual citizenship because that could explain how he was allowed to fly to Israel.

The co-pilot's motive in the alleged attack remains unknown.

"As time passes, the picture is becoming clearer; the attacker underwent Islamist radicalization. He came to crash the plane with its passengers," Netanyahu said in a statement Friday. "We are investigating whether he was dispatched, and whoever sent him will pay a very heavy price."

Netanyahu speculated to CBS News on Wednesday that the incident looked "like a suicide attempt," referring to witnesses who said the co-pilot had tried to jam the plane's equipment instead of stabilizing the aircraft. After passengers subdued the co-pilot, he shouted for someone to kill him, Netanyahu told Fox News on Thursday.

In the same interview with Fox, Netanyahu said "personal information" gathered during ongoing questioning had led Israel to the conclusion that the co-pilot "underwent Islamist radical indoctrination." He did not offer more information.

Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz on Wednesday called the incident "an attempted jihadist terror attack," and referred to the co-pilot as a "terrorist."

President Trump suggested Thursday that the co-pilot may be linked to Iran, "based on what I'm hearing."

"We're working on it right now," Mr. Trump said. "They're being very open with us. I would say the answer, based on what I'm hearing, is yes. But we're working on it right now."

His comments went further than Netanyahu's, who told Fox it was "too early to say" if Iran was involved.

An Israeli security official told CBS News that authorities were investigating the possibility the incident could have been an attempted Sept. 11-style terror attack, and were also probing whether the attacker was working alone. Netanyahu has warned in recent days of unspecified, escalating security threats to Israel and its interests amid its ongoing operations against Iran-allied Hamas in the Gaza Strip and Hezbollah in Lebanon.

The co-pilot was placed under arrest immediately.

He was transferred Thursday from Saudi Arabia to the United Arab Emirates for questioning by Israeli, UAE and Saudi officials, an Israeli official confirmed to CBS News on Friday.

On Wednesday, Netanyahu said the man was "being questioned by the Saudi authorities" and confirmed that Israeli authorities would "join the interrogation and find out what happened there exactly."

Netanyahu has not said what information has led investigators to conclude the co-pilot underwent radicalization.

Editor's note: This story has been updated to reflect that the pilot resigned from Oman Air and wasn't fired.

articles.title: Spoilers: Is social media ruining gig surprises?
articles.summary: Big moments from headline acts are shared online long before many fans see their favourite artists.
articles.body:
Months before you have a chance to see your favourite artist, chances are you already know some of the big moments they have planned.

You'll also probably know the set list, the stage design, and - if you've really been paying attention - where to stand to get the best view.

When it comes to films and TV series, spoilers tend to be guarded against with warnings.

But for many major gigs, there's no escaping a stream of fan videos from the shows if you're online, whether you like it or not.

Last week, US pop star Olivia Rodrigo kicked off her Unraveled tour, and surprises from the show, which scores of fans have paid a lot of money to see, have already been dissected online.

Tours by Harry Styles, Charli XCX and Ariana Grande have also been filmed from every angle and shared over the past few months.

While some fans lap up the opportunity to see what's coming, others are taking extreme measures to preserve the element of surprise.

Aurélia Collins is one of them, spending weeks trying to trick her algorithm into not serving her content about her favourite artists and tapping "not interested" when videos come up, even though she says "it hurts my soul".

It can mean her social media feed is a bit bland, but she tells BBC Newsbeat "it's worth it for the surprise".

The 20-year-old criminology student is a huge One Direction fan and says she just about managed to avoid spoilers for Styles' Together, Together tour over summer.

But when one slipped through the net about Niall Horan before she was able to see his show in London on Saturday - her first time seeing him live after being a fan for 16 years - she was "gutted".

"When I was younger, we couldn't afford to go to events like this and hear live music and because it's such a moment, I really want to take it in," she says.

"I want the full experience, and that includes the element of surprise that people that go to the opening night of the tour can get."

Not all fans think spoilers are a bad thing, though. In fact, Georgia McAdam claims she loves them.

"I'm the type of person that loves to be prepared," the 22-year-old says.

"I love to know what the stage is looking like, what the set list consists of and where to stand."

McAdam's a huge Olivia Rodrigo fan and sees online spoilers more as "teasers". She feels no amount of online videos can ever really take away from the excitement of the real thing.

"Sometimes you get different surprise songs to what's online or you never know what an artist might do," she adds.

Some artists have reacted by switching up their sets in small ways each night to make sure fans coming to later dates still see something unexpected.

Taylor Swift had bespoke outfits and surprise songs during her mammoth Eras tour, Sabrina Carpenter performed unique positions during her song Juno and switched up her Nonsense outro, and Jay-Z has been changing up his set list on his current run.

But the Guardian's deputy music editor Laura Snapes says it's not just fans who can benefit from these twists.

"One way that they can make sure they're staying in the press is by having something different happen in their show every night," Snapes says. "Obviously, it'll be all over TikTok."

Figures shared by TikTok with Newsbeat show posts using #CharliXCX have increased by more than 40% since the singer launched her Music, Fashion, Film tour last month.

If you want to avoid spoilers, there's only one thing you can do, according to Snapes: "You have to not look at TikTok.

"If you want to be surprised, you have to protect yourself from absorbing any of that culture."

Phoebe Bridgers is taking things one step further to make sure fans are surprised at her shows - she's banning phones altogether.

Those attending are required to lock their phones and any recording devices in a special pouch when they enter the venue to see the US singer. Anyone found breaking the rules will be escorted out.

McAdam wouldn't support a ban on phones, saying recording at gigs is "part of the experience" for a lot of fans.

But Collins says she's "not totally against it".

What she'd prefer is to see more spoiler warnings on videos so fans have the option to be surprised if they want.

But even if you know the set list, the staging and the outfits, "you're still probably going to get to see moments of humanity and stuff that's unplanned," Snapes adds.

"I went to the Edinburgh Eras show where Taylor Swift was really snotty and she had to blow her nose. That's not part of the script.

articles.title: China's gold-copper mine built a road from mining waste; one section showed 97% lower deflection after 28 days
articles.summary: Gold mining produces more than the metal that eventually leaves the mine.
articles.body: Gold mining produces more than the metal that eventually leaves the mine. Open-pit operations also generate large quantities of solid waste, including rock, slag and other residues that must be managed and stored. A new study has tested whether some of that material can instead be turned into part of a working mine road. The peer-reviewed study, Sustainable valorization of mine-derived solid wastes into cementitious pavement materials: Mechanical performance and microstructural insights, published in Sustainable Chemistry and Pharmacy in 2026, developed a pavement material made entirely from mine-derived wastes and tested it at the Zijinshan Gold-Copper Mine in Longyan, China. After 28 days of service, the 15% composite-solid-waste pavement section recorded 97.19% lower deflection than a granular blast-slag pavement base. The test roads were exposed to 100-tonne truck traffic and seasonal rainfall.Mining waste in road construction: why mine-derived materials are gaining attentionThe idea of using mining waste in roads is not new. A 2025 review, Sustainable Utilisation of Mining Waste in Road Construction: A Review, published in the Journal of Experimental and Theoretical Analyses, estimates that more than 100 billion tonnes of mining waste are generated each year globally. The review examines the use of materials including tailings, slag and other mining by-products in pavement layers and notes potential benefits from reducing demand for virgin construction materials. At the same time, it identifies variability in waste composition, leaching risks and a lack of standardised design methods as barriers to wider adoption.A separate 2023 review in Minerals, Mining Wastes as Road Construction Material: A Review, found that mine waste has been tested or used in applications ranging from road bases and subbases to embankments and asphalt. It also notes that the approach has not yet been adopted on a large scale, partly because different mines produce materials with very different physical and chemical properties. The 2026 study takes that research into an operating mine. Instead of relying only on laboratory specimens, the researchers constructed field sections using a composite material made from blasting slag and neutralised dreg, amended with additional composite solid waste. The resulting pavement material was derived entirely from mine waste, allowing the researchers to examine its behaviour under actual mine traffic rather than only controlled laboratory loading.Pavement deflection and 100-tonne trucks: what the 97% figure actually showsPavement deflection measures how much a road surface deforms when a load is applied. Lower deflection indicates greater resistance to deformation, which is particularly important for haul roads carrying heavy vehicles repeatedly. At the Zijinshan mine, researchers tested several pavement bases. The field sections were constructed on haul roads at the 670-metre and 730-metre levels of the waste dump area. The roads were exposed to 100-tonne truck traffic, and the field evaluation measured performance after 28 days of service. After 28 days of service, the pavement containing 15% composite solid waste, known as FCBN-15, recorded a deflection of 7.62 hundredths of a millimetre. The granular blasting-slag pavement base after 28 days, designated FCBS, recorded 271.54 hundredths of a millimetre. The researchers calculated that FCBN-15 had 97.19% lower deflection than FCBS. It also showed 63.90% lower deflection than the natural rock pavement and 73.02% lower deflection than the natural soil pavement tested in the study.That does not mean the waste-based road will last 97% longer or require 97% less maintenance. The study measured deformation resistance over a short field period. Still, the result provides field evidence that the material can resist deformation under demanding operating conditions. The researchers also found that performance depended on the amount of composite solid waste used. The 9% formulation showed substantially higher deflection than the 15% formulation after 28 days and deteriorated when subjected to more than three wetting-drying cycles.The 15% formulation showed the lowest deflection in the field test, but it was also more expensive. The authors identified the 9% formulation as offering a balance between performance and material cost, while noting that longer-term field evaluation is still required.Sustainable mine haul roads: carbon emissions and cost still matterMechanical performance was only one part of the study. The researchers also examined environmental and economic factors. Their simplified cradle-to-gate assessment estimated total carbon emissions of 7.466 kilograms of CO₂ per square metre for the 9% composite-solid-waste material and 7.495 kilograms for the 15% formulation. By comparison, cement-stabilised and fly-ash-stabilised materials produced 14.043 and 13.430 kilograms of CO₂ per square metre, respectively.Cost results were more complicated. The researchers calculated material costs ranging from $3.94 per square metre for the 3% formulation to $6.99 for the 15% formulation. The 9% formulation cost $5.86 per square metre, compared with $6.92 for the cement-stabilised base and $6.81 for the fly-ash-stabilised base. The authors concluded that the 9% formulation offered a balance between performance and material cost, rather than finding that the strongest 15% formulation was automatically the cheapest option. The study also included leaching tests. For the 15% formulation, leaching tests measured 0.007 mg/L of cadmium, 0.00003 mg/L of mercury and 0.02 mg/L of chromium. The researchers reported that all three met the groundwater IV standard used in their assessment. These results provide short-term environmental evidence for the tested material, but they do not establish that every type of mining waste would be environmentally suitable for road construction.What still needs testing before mining waste roads become widespreadThe biggest limitation is time. The field evaluation in the 2026 study was conducted after 28 days of service, meaning it does not establish how the pavement will perform after years of repeated heavy-truck loading, seasonal weather and changes in mine operations. The authors themselves describe the field evaluation as a short-term assessment. That limitation is important because mining waste is not a single material. Its chemical composition, particle size, strength and environmental behaviour can vary considerably between mines. The 2025 road-construction review similarly identifies material variability, leaching and the absence of standardised design protocols as unresolved issues.Other research is also moving beyond laboratory testing. A 2026 review titled Geopolymerization of Mine Tailings for Pavement Applications: Properties, Limitations and Future Directions, notes that field conditions can produce lower strength than laboratory specimens because of differences in placement and curing. It also highlights the need for repeated-loading and long-term durability studies before such materials can be assessed for broader pavement use. For now, the Zijinshan trial provides a useful piece of field evidence rather than a universal solution. It shows that mine-derived waste can be engineered into a pavement base capable of resisting substantial deformation under heavy mine traffic, while also reducing the calculated carbon footprint relative to the conventional materials tested. Whether the approach can be safely and economically reproduced at other mines will depend on the composition of their waste, local environmental requirements and longer-term performance under real traffic.You use AI every day. articles.title: Saudi Arabia readies 100,000 Yemeni troops for Houthi assault: Can fragmented Yemeni forces retake Bab el-Mandeb?
articles.summary: Saudi Arabia is preparing an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen, with Riyadh weighing a limited coastal assault around the Bab el-Mandeb
articles.body: Saudi Arabia is preparing an offensive against Iran-backed Houthi forces in Yemen, with Riyadh weighing a limited coastal assault around the Bab el-Mandeb Strait or a broader multi-front operation.According to Reuters, the offensive could be launched in the coming weeks and would be led by Yemeni forces and backed by Saudi air strikes.The report, citing six people familiar with the preparations, said more than 100,000 Yemeni troops could be mobilised depending on the scale of the operation, while the timing remains uncertain, with estimates ranging from within a week to after the US midterm elections in early November.The immediate objective of the planned offensive is to reverse the Houthis' rapid gains last month, when the group advanced down Yemen's Red Sea coast and seized control of the Bab el-Mandeb Strait, according to people familiar with the Saudi preparations cited by Reuters.Bab el-Mandeb is the southern exit of the Red Sea and a key shipping route between the Mediterranean and Asia. The route has gained greater importance this year as an alternative to the Strait of Hormuz, which has been effectively closed by the Iran conflict.Michael Ratney, a former US ambassador to Saudi Arabia, said he expected the operation to be more limited than the Saudi-led intervention in Yemen that began in 2015.“Ideally, it would be a fairly limited operation to retake coastal areas and get back to normal maritime traffic,” Ratney said, according to Reuters.Ratney's assessment points to the immediate military objective being focused on the Red Sea coast rather than an attempt to defeat the Houthis across Yemen.Saudi Arabia's problem on the groundThe biggest challenge for Riyadh is the condition of the Yemeni forces that would lead the ground offensive. The force is a collection of factions armed and trained by Saudi Arabia and the UAE rather than a unified military, and those groups have competing political and territorial interests.Yemen analyst Mohammed Albasha told Reuters that many anti-Houthi forces are still “not organised or prepared” for the sustained offensive needed to push back the Houthis, who are applying pressure across several fronts.The anti-Houthi camp was further fractured last winter when UAE-backed southern fighters clashed with Saudi-backed forces after trying to seize territory in eastern Yemen.Ali Shihabi, a Saudi political analyst close to government thinking, also said the outcome would depend on the performance of the local forces, with the ground campaign moving from defending positions to going on the offensive.Where are Saudi Arabia's allies?Saudi Arabia's allies are backing Riyadh mainly through intelligence, equipment and defensive support rather than direct combat in Yemen.The United States, Saudi Arabia's most powerful ally, is providing military advisers and intelligence, including targeting information for Saudi air operations.However, Reuters reported that President Donald Trump had previously rejected Saudi requests for direct US military support, including air strikes, leaving Riyadh to conduct the air campaign itself.A separate pillar of Saudi security is the Mecca Joint Defence Agreement, signed by Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey on August 7.The pact says an armed attack on one of the three countries will be treated as an attack on all. But Pakistan has so far stopped short of committing combat forces to Yemen.Islamabad has instead sent air-defence systems, light artillery, drones and anti-drone equipment, while 30,000 to 40,000 Pakistani troops are deployed inside Saudi Arabia for border defence and missile and drone interception.Turkey has also supplied military equipment and Turkish drones are being used over Yemen, while France has announced defensive systems and troops for the protection of Saudi Arabia's Red Sea port of Yanbu.The military chiefs of Saudi Arabia, Pakistan and Turkey met in Riyadh on September 25 to discuss the situation, while Pakistan's foreign minister said on October 2 that the three countries would hold an emergency meeting in Riyadh next week.You use AI every day. articles.summary: Convicted murderer Christa Pike remains in critical condition after Tennessee's attempt to execute her failed, leaving her unconscious and dependent on a
articles.body: Convicted murderer Christa Pike remains in critical condition after Tennessee's attempt to execute her failed, leaving her unconscious and dependent on a ventilator, her lawyers said Friday.Pike is being treated in hospital, where doctors are working to keep her alive and remove the lethal drug pentobarbital from her system, according to her attorneys. They made the disclosure in an emergency court filing seeking an order requiring Tennessee's Department of Correction to preserve evidence from Wednesday night's failed execution.The 50-year-old received two doses of pentobarbital, but the drug did not kill her. Her lawyers said she has suffered significant injuries to both arms and remains intubated, meaning a breathing tube has been placed in her airway and connected to a ventilator to help her breathe.The filing gave the most detailed account so far of what happened during the execution. Pike's lawyers said problems with intravenous access prevented the drugs from being properly delivered."At no point did any member of the execution team realize that the IV lines were not correctly placed or that the veins had blown and that the pentobarbital was, in whole or in part, entering Ms. Pike’s body," Pike's lawyers said in a filing in the Chancery Court for the State of Tennessee Twentieth Judicial District.Pike's attorneys had warned Tennessee officials and courts before the execution about difficulties involving intravenous access, which is needed to administer the lethal injection.Tennessee Governor Bill Lee has said the execution was carried out according to the state's established protocol. However, it was the second failed execution in the state this year.Lee has since halted further executions in Tennessee for the remainder of 2026 and ordered an independent review into what happened.Pike was convicted of killing her 19-year-old classmate, Colleen Slemmer, in 1995. Pike was 18 at the time of the killing.She had been scheduled to become the first woman executed in Tennessee in more than 200 years.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Hawaii’s picturesque Hōlei Sea Arch collapses into the ocean
articles.summary: The Google Maps red pin for the Hōlei Sea Arch, a rugged, 90-foot bow formed by 550-year-old lava flows and the prolonged sculpture of the salty Pacific, now states, “Permanently closed.”
articles.body: The Google Maps red pin for the Hōlei Sea Arch, a rugged, 90-foot bow formed by 550-year-old lava flows and the prolonged sculpture of the salty Pacific, now states, “Permanently closed.” On Thursday, the National Park Service said the picturesque arch at Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park on the Big Island had collapsed sometime between Sept. 23 and Sunday, around the time a tropical cyclone sent sizable swell into the coast. “The exact time of the collapse is unknown and could have occurred when the park was temporarily closed during Tropical Storm Nolo,” the park service said in a statement. The park service lamented the collapse of the natural feature it said was likely rooted in lava flows roughly half a millennium ago and then slowly shaped by the reduction of a roiling sea. It also said some who want to see what’s left of the Hōlei Sea Arch have stepped too close to the edge of surrounding cliffs — as seen on social media. The park service warned sightseers to keep a safe distance from the eroding coastline, where they could put “themselves and first responders at great risk of falling and drowning off the rough, wave-swept coast,” it said. “Visitors are urged to stay back from the unstable coastal cliff edges which drop off vertically into the ocean and present a serious falling hazard,” it said. The collapse was a long time coming, the park service said, with the 2018 Kīlauea eruption shaking the ground enough to damage the arch’s neighboring cliffs. New cracks on the feature and its surroundings in early 2020 inspired Hawai’i Volcanoes National Park officials to move the Hōlei Sea Arch’s viewing area farther from land’s end, the park service said. “Later that year, massive surf from Tropical Storm Darby broke off a chunk of rock from the lower part of the arch,” it said. The U.S. Geological Survey said the arch is a product of “differential erosion by ocean waves” whereby the sea works to first remove material along cracks and weaker sections of basalt rock. “Every day the ocean crashes against the pillar of the arch, eroding it a little more,” it said in its entry for the arch. “One day, it will be gone.”

articles.title: Munich Oktoberfest ride gives women free shorts amid thousands of upskirting videos
articles.summary: A popular ride at Munich's Oktoberfest has become the centre of a growing controversy over voyeuristic videos, with its operator handing out free cycling
articles.body: A popular ride at Munich's Oktoberfest has become the centre of a growing controversy over voyeuristic videos, with its operator handing out free cycling shorts to women to help protect them from being filmed under their skirts.The Teufelsrad, or Devil's Wheel, is one of the oldest attractions at the annual beer festival. Its large circular platform spins at increasing speeds, eventually throwing riders off. The movement can cause skirts and dresses to fly up, making people on the ride vulnerable to being filmed from below.Thousands of videos showing women on the attraction have appeared online, with some reportedly attracting millions of views. German broadcaster BR reported that one woman earned €9,000 from a single clip.Thousands of videos circulating onlineAt least 32,000 videos featuring women on the Teufelsrad have been circulated, according to Munich daily Süddeutsche Zeitung. Some have apparently been watched millions of times.The videos often show women wearing traditional dirndl dresses with their underwear visible. Some images have also been digitally manipulated to make the women appear naked, according to BR.BR's investigation found that a group of professional YouTubers from Ukraine and several people from Bavaria were behind the videos.Filming under someone's skirt is illegal in Germany and can carry a prison sentence of up to two years. However, critics say the law does not cover every situation in which intimate images are captured.Josephine Ballon, head of German non-profit organisation Hate Aid, which supports victims of digital violence, said the existing law does not offer enough protection. She said there are plans for new legislation, but the current law "applies only when you film under the skirt", meaning it may not apply when a skirt simply flies up and someone photographs what is visible.Ballon also warned that new devices such as camera glasses could create additional risks.Ride operator gives women free cycling shortsElisabeth Polaczy, who runs the Teufelsrad, told the BBC that she has been giving women and girls wearing dresses free cycling shorts for the past three years.She said she has handed out more than 100 pairs during this year's Oktoberfest."I want to do everything I can to make people feel secure."Polaczy, who is 80, said providing the shorts costs her money but gives her peace of mind.The Teufelsrad tent displays signs and police posters in both German and English warning visitors against filming under people's skirts. However, Polaczy said it is impossible to monitor everyone using a smartphone in the crowded area.Some waitresses working at this year's festival have also started wearing cycling shorts beneath their dirndls.Police step up warnings as influencers face new rulesBavarian police have been running a poster campaign at Oktoberfest since 2025 to warn visitors about upskirting, a spokesman told the BBC.Police arrested a 45-year-old Swiss man this year after he was allegedly caught using his phone to film under a German woman's dirndl. There were 10 arrests for upskirting at the festival last year and seven in 2024.Ballon said people who upload intimate images online should face consequences, as should platforms that host such material.The issue comes as Munich authorities are also tightening rules for influencers and content creators who make money from filming at Oktoberfest.The city has banned live streaming from the festival and requires people who want to film there to obtain a permit for a fee. Hundreds of permits have been issued this year to influencers who earn money through activities such as product placements and sponsorships.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.body: The complainant in the alleged sexual assault case at Cornell University is “under siege” on social media, where people are attempting to identify her, according to her lawyer.“She’s under siege on social media, where people are trying to identify her,” her lawyer, Thomas Giuffra, told CNN.In a separate interview with CBS, Giuffra said the woman, called “Jane Doe” in court documents, was “incapable of consent” because she was “completely, grossly intoxicated” when she arrived at a Cornell University fraternity house in Ithaca, New York, on October 19, 2024, when she was allegedly sexually assaulted there by seven men."Jane Doe had been pressured into taking the drug ketamine before she was raped. She was 20 at the time... she was unable to provide consent because she was intoxicated when she arrived at the fraternity house," he added.Giuffra’s comments come as social media feeds have filled with women seeking to protect the Cornell accuser’s identity by posting videos of themselves under the title “I am Jane Doe.”The posts are intended not only to make it more difficult to identify her through online searches, but also to show solidarity. Many of the women have shared their own experiences of sexual assault.Efforts to rally around Jane Doe intensified after a political commentator vowed to reveal her identity, arguing that it was “unfair” for her to remain anonymous while the men she accused were publicly identified, despite not having been charged with a crime.Online sleuths have also attempted to locate the addresses of the so-called "Cornell Seven," resulting in at least one case of mistaken identity.An active-duty US Marine Corps sergeant who shared the same name as one of the men was mistakenly served with the woman’s lawsuit, prompting a torrent of abuse and threats.No criminal charges were initially filed in the case. The investigation was later reopened after Jane Doe filed a civil lawsuit that brought her allegations into the national spotlight and revived the possibility of criminal charges.New York Governor Kathy Hochul has appointed state Attorney General Letitia James to take over the investigation.You use AI every day. articles.title: African Parks spent 20 years testing conservation in Malawi; its new model now covers 1.37 million hectares across three African parks
articles.summary: For more than two decades, African Parks has been working to restore and manage wildlife landscapes in Malawi, beginning with Majete Wildlife Reserve in
articles.body: For more than two decades, African Parks has been working to restore and manage wildlife landscapes in Malawi, beginning with Majete Wildlife Reserve in 2003. That long-running conservation work has now become the testing ground for a different question, how can the ecological health of protected areas be measured in a way that also helps attract long-term funding? The organisation developed the Verifiable Nature Unit (VNU) with The Landbanking Group as an outcomes-based system for measuring, reporting and verifying changes in nature. The African Parks Organisation says the first VNU pilot was launched at Majete Wildlife Reserve, Malawi, after more than 20 years of conservation management. The model has since expanded beyond Malawi, with VNU projects in three large African parks covering a combined 1.37 million hectares.Majete became the testing ground for the new conservation modelAfrican Parks signed its first management mandate for Majete Wildlife Reserve with the Malawian government in 2003. The reserve covers some parts of south-western Malawi and underwent extensive restoration, including the reintroduction of wildlife species that had been depleted from the area.Over the following two decades, African Parks says more than 3,000 animals representing 17 species were reintroduced at Majete. Rhino reintroductions began in 2003, followed by elephants in 2006, lions in 2012, giraffes in 2018, cheetahs in 2019 and African wild dogs in 2021. The organisation also developed infrastructure and worked with communities surrounding the reserve.That long period of management gave African Parks what it describes as an ideal proof of concept for the VNU. The first VNU pilot was launched at Majete, where 711 VNUs were issued in 2024 and reissued in 2025.Each VNU represents a square kilometre of natureThe VNU is designed to turn ecological outcomes into a standardised unit that can be measured over time. African Parks defines each VNU as one square kilometre of land whose ecological integrity has been maintained or improved over a specified period.Rather than simply measuring how much land exists inside a protected area, the system looks at whether the condition of that land is being maintained or improved. African Parks says each VNU is assessed annually using two principal indicators are habitat intactness and indicator species.Habitat intactness tracks changes caused by pressures such as settlement expansion, deforestation and agricultural conversion. Indicator species are monitored for their presence and abundance as a measure of broader ecosystem health. The system also uses observation, machine learning, third-party verification and a digital system for issuing and reporting VNUs.The model expanded to 1.37 million hectaresAfter the Majete pilot, African Parks began testing VNUs in three additional national parks, Odzala-Kokoua in the Republic of the Congo, Garamba in the Democratic Republic of the Congo, and Zakouma in Chad.According to African Parks, VNUs issued for these three parks in 2025 and again in 2026 cover a combined 1.37 million hectares, or 13,700 square kilometres. The expansion takes the system from its original Malawi proof of concept into several much larger and ecologically different landscapes.The VNU is not itself a biodiversity credit. African Parks describes it as an independently verified measurement of ecosystem integrity that can underpin different funding mechanisms, including outcomes-based grants, nature or biodiversity credits, nature-linked financial instruments and payments for ecosystem services. During the pilot phase, VNUs are being used through bilateral agreements with funders rather than as tradeable units.African Parks wants conservation outcomes to become measurableThe organisation's broader aim is to connect funding to measurable conservation results. Instead of funding being based only on activities carried out in a park, the VNU framework is intended to show whether ecological integrity is actually being maintained or improved.African Parks says the next stage will involve expanding the methodology into community-managed landscapes surrounding the pilot parks. The organisation plans to test whether verified conservation outcomes can also help support community development and provide incentives for protecting natural areas outside formally protected parks.For African Parks, Majete therefore serves two roles, it is a long-running example of conservation management in Malawi and the first testing ground for a system designed to measure the ecological results of that work. The approach has now moved beyond the reserve, with VNU projects spanning 1.37 million hectares across Odzala-Kokoua, Garamba and Zakouma.You use AI every day. Now get your AI Quotient. articles.title: Posted about niqab, ‘ruined women’: Omani co-pilot's social media trail reveals radical ideology
articles.summary: Deleted social media posts by Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar aboard a Flydubai flight, have
articles.body: Deleted social media posts by Hamam al-Hammami, the Omani co-pilot accused of attacking Indian pilot Captain Smit Machchhar aboard a Flydubai flight, have offered a glimpse into his views on women, religion and mixed-gender workplaces.CNN, citing multiple sources familiar with the matter, reported that al-Hammami had described difficulties finding a prospective wife who would agree to wear a niqab and stop working after marriage. In another deleted post, he questioned the impact of mixed-gender workplaces on women, writing that religious women could be “ruined” in such environments.The posts were part of nearly 3,000 deleted tweets from 2021 and 2022 that CNN analysed using an AI-powered semantic search model. The revelations come as authorities investigate the September 30 incident, in which al-Hammami allegedly attacked Machchhar inside the cockpit of a Dubai-Tel Aviv flight, causing the aircraft to plunge sharply before passengers and crew overpowered him.Hammami also posted disturbing content about killing Jews online, according to an Israeli official cited by the Times of Israel. “He talks about killing Jews,” the official said, adding that his social media activity indicated he had been radicalised into a jihadist ideology. Israeli outlet i24 also reported that he allegedly possessed anti-Israeli literature. Authorities are investigating whether the attack was linked to terrorist activity or a specific intent to target Jewish passengers.What did al-Hammami post about women?According to CNN, one deleted post from February 2022 discussed his mother's efforts to find him a wife who would accept his conditions, including wearing a niqab and giving up work after marriage.The post claimed that several prospective families had rejected those conditions before his mother told them that her son was a pilot, after which they allegedly changed their minds.In another post from January 2022, al-Hammami criticised mixed-gender workplaces and questioned their effect on women. CNN described the deleted Twitter account as showing deeply religious and misogynistic views, although the posts themselves represent his past online statements and do not, by themselves, establish his motive in the Flydubai incident.CNN also reported that two posts appeared on a LinkedIn account bearing al-Hammami's name around nine hours after Wednesday's incident. It was unclear whether he had posted them himself or whether they had been scheduled earlier.One post contained cockpit footage of Boeing 737 Max aircraft and images of Israeli airline planes. The video ended with photographs of former al-Qaeda leader Ayman al-Zawahiri and Humam Khalil Abu-Mulal al-Balawi, who carried out a 2009 suicide bombing that killed nine people, including seven CIA personnel.A second post featured an AI-generated image depicting Islam's three holy sites in Mecca, Medina and Jerusalem, accompanied by a poem about rejecting humiliation, not fearing death and defending one's dignity.Why was he removed from flying?The social media revelations have emerged alongside reports that al-Hammami had previously faced concerns over his suitability to fly.CNN reported that al-Hammami, an Omani citizen born in the UAE to an Omani father and Syrian mother, had worked for Oman Air for around seven years. Two sources told the network that he was removed from flight-related duties after concerns about extremist views and was moved to another role at the airline.CBS News, citing sources, separately reported that Omani government surveillance had detected visits to radical websites during his pilot training, prompting Oman Air to move him to desk duties. He subsequently left the airline.His LinkedIn profile, which has since been deleted, said he left Oman Air in February 2025 and later worked for Royal Air Maroc between June 2025 and January 2026. CNN said a source confirmed the profile belonged to the Flydubai pilot.Al Arabiya English also reported, citing sources, that al-Hammami had previously been barred from flying in Oman over concerns about extremist views, while other reports have raised questions about the extent of vetting when he later joined Flydubai.Israeli Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu has said al-Hammami appeared to have undergone “Islamist radical indoctrination”, though he has not publicly provided evidence supporting that assertion.You use AI every day. articles.title: Security lapse Israel overlooked? Over 12 Omani pilots flew to Tel Aviv despite ban
articles.summary: Israeli authorities are facing tough questions over how an Omani pilot was able to fly into Tel Aviv despite a rule barring pilots from countries without
articles.body: Israeli authorities are facing tough questions over how an Omani pilot was able to fly into Tel Aviv despite a rule barring pilots from countries without diplomatic relations with Israel, according to a report by Channel 12.The issue came to light after a hijacking attempt was made on a flydubai flight on Wednesday when its Omani co-pilot allegedly attacked the captain, Smit Machchhar, and attempted to deliberately crash the aircraft.Israeli passengers, the captain and other pilots on board intervened, allowing the plane to make an emergency landing in Saudi Arabia. Most of the passengers were Israeli and were later flown from Saudi Arabia to Israel.Over 12 Omani pilots flew into IsraelOman does not have diplomatic relations with Israel. According to the report, rules introduced after the 2020 Abraham Accords prohibit pilots from countries that do not have relations with Israel from flying into the country.However, Channel 12 reported that dozens of Omani pilots had flown into Israel in recent years while working for foreign airlines.The report said Israeli authorities had largely relied on airlines themselves to ensure that pilots from countries without diplomatic ties with Israel did not operate flights into the country.Channel 12 reported that the Shin Bet security service did not independently investigate the nationalities or backgrounds of flydubai pilots. Instead, it had asked the airline not to use pilots from countries that do not have diplomatic relations with Israel.“The Shin Bet has all the means to know, within five minutes, who all of the pilots on the Dubai airline are, and they simply chose to turn a blind eye,” the network quoted an anonymous airline industry official as saying. “In Israel, they expected the airline to be reliable enough, so they didn’t conduct reviews in recent years.”Israel's Transportation Ministry said the Shin Bet had not issued a specific warning about flydubai, apart from requesting increased baggage checks, according to the report.Security procedures now under scrutinyThe incident has prompted authorities to examine how flight crews from foreign airlines are cleared to enter Israel. Channel 12 reported that the Transportation Ministry and its Center for Aviation Security Operations, which was established in recent years to oversee and monitor the entry of flight crews, will be examined as part of the investigation.The State Comptroller's Office had already recommended in 2024 that the government review security procedures related to air travel.The report also pointed to an earlier dispute between the Shin Bet and Israeli airlines El Al, IsraAir and Arkia. In July, the security service barred the three carriers from landing in Dubai because of concerns over regional tensions linked to the war with Iran.Although that decision involved Israeli airlines rather than foreign carriers, Channel 12 reported that applying similarly strict security measures to foreign airlines could potentially have helped prevent Wednesday's incident.Investigation points to possible terror motiveInvestigations into the attack are continuing in Israel, the United Arab Emirates and Saudi Arabia. The Shin Bet and Mossad are also reportedly cooperating with security agencies in the two countries.Saudi Arabia said the captain and co-pilot, who were treated in hospital for their injuries, left for Abu Dhabi on Thursday after receiving medical clearance.Initial information shared with Israeli authorities reportedly suggested that the co-pilot may have attacked for nationalist reasons, raising the possibility that the incident was treated as a terror attack. The assessment was reportedly based partly on statements the co-pilot made to Saudi investigators, along with other information gathered during the probe.Israeli PM Benjamin Netanyahu said earlier Thursday that the Omani first officer “underwent Islamist radical indoctrination.” Channel 12 said that assessment was based on information from two Israeli sources familiar with the Saudi investigation.The motive has not been independently established, and investigations by authorities in the three countries remain ongoing.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 1902, Hanoi paid people for rat tails to fight plague; more than 55 million tails were collected, but the rats were still alive
articles.summary: In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi introduced a rat bounty during an outbreak of bubonic plague, offering one cent for every rat tail submitted
articles.body: In 1902, French colonial authorities in Hanoi introduced a rat bounty during an outbreak of bubonic plague, offering one cent for every rat tail submitted as proof of a kill. Within a year, more than 55 million rat tails had been collected. But the enormous number of tails did not mean that millions of rats had actually been eliminated. Officials eventually found tailless rats still moving around the city, revealing how people had learned to claim the reward without killing the animals. The episode, known as the Great Hanoi Rat Massacre, is highlighted in a 2026 review published in npj Biodiversity as an example of how financial incentives designed to control unwanted species can produce unintended results.Hanoi's rat bounty began during a plague outbreakThe rat campaign took place in Hanoi, then part of French Indochina, during the Third Plague Pandemic. Historical research by historian Michael G. Vann has documented the French colonial administration's efforts to control the city's rat population in 1902. The campaign was closely connected to the growing concern over plague in Hanoi and the discovery that rats were moving through the city's sewer system.The 2026 review, titled Society's struggle with unwanted species: what centuries of history reveal about species bounty programs, describes the Hanoi programme as a public bounty scheme. Instead of requiring hunters to present an entire dead rat, authorities accepted a severed tail as proof and paid one cent for each tail. The arrangement created a simple incentive: the more tails a person submitted, the more money they could receive. But the system also created a loophole because the proof required by the authorities did not necessarily demonstrate that the rat itself had been killed.More than 55 million tails were submittedAccording to the 2026 npj Biodiversity review, more than 55 million severed rat tails were collected over the course of a year. On paper, the figure suggested an enormous campaign against Hanoi's rats. The results on the streets told a different story. Government officials began noticing rats that were alive but had no tails. The review explains that rat catchers had discovered they could cut off a rat's tail, collect the bounty and then release the animal.That meant the same rat could remain alive after generating a payment. More importantly, the surviving animal could reproduce, creating the possibility of future rats that could also become a source of bounty payments. The episode illustrates what the researchers call a form of fraudulent behaviour in species bounty programmes: not killing the target species. Rather than achieving the intended reduction in the population, the financial incentive could encourage participants to keep the target animals alive.The problem was not simply that people cheatedThe Hanoi episode is significant because it demonstrates a broader problem with bounty schemes. The 2026 review found that financial rewards can change how people interact with the species being targeted. The researchers examined historical and contemporary bounty programmes involving at least 283 species across 449 programmes in 60 countries. Their review covers roughly eight centuries, with examples involving mammals, birds, fish, reptiles, plants, insects and other groups.The authors identify several ways such schemes can go wrong. Participants may submit fraudulent proof, claim rewards for non-target species, harvest animals outside the permitted area or period, or manipulate the programme in ways that allow the target species to survive or even increase. The Hanoi case falls into the last category. The researchers specifically use it as an example of participants claiming a reward while leaving the target animal alive.Hanoi was not the only example of a bounty going wrongThe review identifies other historical cases in which bounty programmes produced unintended consequences. In Britain, for example, a grey squirrel bounty was discontinued in 1958 after authorities concluded that the scheme had not successfully controlled the squirrel population. A contemporary statement in the UK Parliament said the Forestry Commissioners had decided to end the programme because it had not proved successful in controlling grey squirrels. The review also describes cases in which hunters released adult female wolves from traps so that the animals could continue breeding and future bounty payments could be generated.Another famous example is the so-called "cobra effect", a story about a British colonial bounty for cobras in India. According to the widely repeated account, people began breeding cobras to collect the reward and later released them when the programme was cancelled. However, that story should not be presented as an established historical fact. Recent historical examination has questioned whether the Delhi cobra-breeding episode actually occurred as traditionally described. The 2026 npj Biodiversity review itself presents it as an example of the phenomenon, but the underlying historical evidence is considerably less secure than the documented Hanoi case.What the Hanoi rats reveal about bounty programmesThe researchers behind the 2026 review do not argue that every bounty programme is ineffective. Their assessment is broader: bounty schemes vary considerably in their design, implementation and outcomes. Some are carefully planned, while others have been introduced with limited investigation of whether they can actually achieve their intended goal. Financial rewards can increase participation, but they can also encourage behaviour that works against the programme's objective.The authors identified bounty programmes motivated by economic concerns, ecological damage and human health, among other reasons. They conclude that such programmes can remain one tool for managing unwanted species, but their design and monitoring matter. That makes the Hanoi episode more than an unusual story about 55 million rat tails. The extraordinary number of tails collected did not automatically translate into an equivalent number of dead rats. Instead, the reward system created a new incentive for participants to exploit the difference between the evidence required for payment and the outcome the government actually wanted. More than a century later, the case remains one of the clearest historical examples of how a policy designed to remove a problem can create incentives that allow the problem to persist.You use AI every day. articles.title: In 2000, a broken water main flooded an abandoned Dallas rail tunnel; the disaster damaged two federal buildings and led to a $2.33 million settlement
articles.summary: In September 2000, a routine construction project beneath downtown Dallas turned into a major flooding incident after a pressurised water main was damaged
articles.body: In September 2000, a routine construction project beneath downtown Dallas turned into a major flooding incident after a pressurised water main was damaged beneath Young Street. Millions of gallons of treated water poured into an abandoned railway tunnel, eventually reaching two nearby federal buildings. According to the US Department of Justice, the Santa Fe Federal Building was left with about 12 feet of water, while the Earle Cabell Federal Building and US Courthouse also suffered flooding in their basement areas. The buildings were temporarily closed, and the US government later pursued compensation from the construction companies involved. Four years after the incident, a federal jury found Dynamic Cable Construction Company and Reata Construction Company liable for the damage. The dispute eventually ended with a $2.33 million settlement.An unexpected tunnel disrupted fibre-optic work in DallasThe work that preceded the flooding involved the installation of fibre-optic conduits beneath Dallas streets. Dynamic Cable Construction Company had a contract with the City of Dallas for the work, while Reata Construction Company was also involved in the project.According to the US government's case, the companies had not obtained the relevant city maps and design plans before carrying out the underground work. Those documents could have shown the location of existing water utilities.The drilling operation then encountered something unexpected. Beneath Young Street was an abandoned Santa Fe Railroad tunnel, around 20 feet deep and 50 feet wide. Rather than stopping to establish what utilities were nearby, the work continued without consulting the city's water records for the area.Millions of gallons flooded federal buildings through a hidden tunnelA 30-inch pressurised underground water main was broken during the work. Between 30 million and 40 million gallons of treated water escaped, entering the abandoned railway tunnel and spreading into the surrounding area. The tunnel connected with the federal buildings, creating a route for the floodwater to move underground. Water pressure eventually caused the sealed concrete block entrance to collapse, allowing the flooding to reach the basement of the Santa Fe Federal Building.The water did not remain confined there. It also entered the basement and sub-basement of the Earle Cabell Federal Building and US Courthouse at 1100 Commerce Street. Above ground, the incident affected the central business district around Young, Jackson and Griffin streets. Water emerged through breaks in the tunnel ceiling and collected across parts of downtown.A 12-foot flood forced the Santa Fe Federal Building to closeThe Santa Fe Federal Building sustained particularly extensive flooding. Water reached roughly 12 feet inside the building, and the facility remained closed for seven days. The Earle Cabell Federal Building and US Courthouse was closed for two days while the effects of the flooding were dealt with.The timing added an unusual detail to the episode. Dallas was experiencing record-setting heat, while much of the city was subject to some form of water restriction because of limited rainfall. Yet the damaged main released tens of millions of gallons of treated water into the tunnel and streets.The federal government, through the General Services Administration, subsequently sought to recover the cost of repairing the affected property.Construction companies appealed after the 2004 jury verdictThe case eventually reached a federal jury in Dallas. In November 2004, jurors found Dynamic Cable Construction Company and Reata Construction Company responsible for compensating the US government for the property damage.Reportedly, the resulting judgment was $2,212,636.72, with additional costs and interest. The construction companies challenged the outcome and appealed the case to the US Court of Appeals for the Fifth Circuit. The dispute did not end with an appellate ruling. While the appeal was still pending, the parties reached a settlement.US government recovered $2.33 million over the 2000 Dallas floodingThe final agreement provided the US government with essentially the full amount owed at that stage of the proceedings. The settlement funds received by the government totalled $2.33 million.The money represented compensation for damage to federal property caused by the 2000 flooding. The case was announced by US Attorney Richard B. Roper for the Northern District of Texas as an example of the government's efforts to recover losses involving federal property.You use AI every day. articles.title: The California ranch where Shirley Temple married Charles Black in 1950 has sold for $2.45 million; the 1940 adobe home spans 2,180 square feet and remained tied to her husband’s family for decades
articles.summary: A Monterey, California, ranch house with a quiet claim to Hollywood history has changed hands for $2.45 million.
articles.body: A Monterey, California, ranch house with a quiet claim to Hollywood history has changed hands for $2.45 million. Built in 1940 as a weekend retreat for the family of naval officer Charles Black, the adobe home is where child star Shirley Temple married Black in 1950 in a simple ceremony in front of a fireplace. The 2,180-square-foot residence, which remained connected to Black’s family for decades, recently listed after its current owners carried out careful upgrades while preserving its historic character, according to a report by Realtor.com.A weekend cottage with cinematic tiesThe house, known in family circles as the Black family cottage Mesita, sits in what was once an open mesa above Monterey. It was designed as a single-level horizontal ranch with a tile roof, white adobe walls, and French doors opening onto a loggia that runs the full length of the home. In June 1941, just a year after construction, the property was featured on the cover of Sunset Magazine, highlighting its blend of Spanish mission and New England influences.Shirley Temple described the cottage in her 1988 autobiography as a white-washed hideaway whose architecture reflected Monterey’s historical heritage. She noted the mix of adobe brick and curved red-roof tiles associated with Spanish mission fathers, along with wooden slat shutters and mullioned window panes reminiscent of New England. For Temple, the setting offered a sylvan backdrop that felt both intimate and timeless.The 1950 wedding that made it famousTemple met Charles Black at a party in Hawaii in 1950, when he was a naval officer and avid surfer. Their courtship moved quickly because Black was scheduled for deployment to Korea shortly after Temple’s divorce from her first husband was finalised. She had hoped to marry in a gothic Catholic chapel near her in-laws’ cottage, but the reverend declined to perform the ceremony due to her recent divorce.Undeterred, the couple held a modest wedding at the Black family cottage. Temple later recalled that they were married by a local justice of the peace in front of a fireplace decorated with boughs. After the ceremony, they drove to a hotel using aliases to avoid press attention. The marriage lasted until Black’s death in 2005, making it the longest and most stable chapter of Temple’s personal life.Adobe construction with modern resilienceThe home spans 2,180 square feet and includes three bedrooms, a formal dining room, original hardwood floors, and wood-burning fireplaces. An enclosed garden shaded by towering oak trees adds to the property’s sense of privacy and calm. Today the house sits on a residential block in the Aguajito Oaks neighborhood, close to sprawling golf courses and the natural landscapes that first attracted the Black family, as per the report.Though adobe structures can settle over time, this house has remained remarkably stable. Charles Black’s father, James B. Black, who served as president and chairman of Pacific Gas and Electric Company, reinforced the structure with concrete and steel during construction. That reinforcement has helped the home maintain its integrity for more than eight decades, according to the listing agent.Recent upgrades honour the original designThe current sellers, a couple known for creating plastic palm trees used in theme parks and movie sets such as Jurassic Park, purchased the property in 2022 for $1.81 million from the estate of its previous long-time owners. Over the last few years they replaced all the doors and windows and upgraded the electrical and plumbing systems while keeping the home’s historic feel intact.Listing agent David O’Neil of Sotheby’s International Realty noted that the combination of thick adobe walls and a clay tile roof helps regulate indoor temperatures naturally. He said the house can stay comfortable without needing a heater in many conditions, a feature that blends historic building wisdom with modern expectations for efficiency.A property that bridges eras and storiesFor decades the house remained tied to Charles Black’s family, serving as a quiet anchor through changes in Monterey’s landscape and in the lives of its famous residents. Its sale marks a new chapter for a property that has witnessed both Hollywood glamour and ordinary family moments. The blend of cinematic history, architectural character, and coastal location continues to draw interest from buyers seeking homes with narrative depth.The $2.45 million sale price reflects not only the home’s size and location but also its unique place in cultural memory. For fans of classic Hollywood, the ranch is a tangible link to Shirley Temple’s transition from child star to wife, mother, and later diplomat. For preservation-minded buyers, it is an example of how mid-century adobe design can be updated without losing its soul.Why this sale matters beyond the price tagReal estate with celebrity provenance often commands attention, but this property stands out because of how closely its story aligns with Temple’s own life narrative. The fireplace where she and Black exchanged vows remains a focal point, and the surrounding rooms carry the quiet weight of a marriage that endured for more than half a century. That continuity gives the home an emotional resonance that few listings can match.At the same time, the house illustrates how historic properties can be useful and attractive through careful stewardship. Doors, windows, electrical and plumbing have been upgraded to provide modern comfort; meanwhile, original floors, fireplaces and adobe massing retain the character that originally attracted the Black family to the site. For Monterey, the sale is another reminder that its architectural heritage includes not just grand estates but also modest cottages with extraordinary stories.Ready to Make a Smarter Property Decision? articles.title: IIT Bombay suicide: What Professor Suryanaraya Doolla told investigators during eight-hour questioning
articles.summary: NEW DELHI: IIT Bombay Professor Suryanarayana Doolla told the Mumbai Police Crime Branch that he had followed the institute’s prescribed guidelines and
articles.body: NEW DELHI: IIT Bombay Professor Suryanarayana Doolla told the Mumbai Police Crime Branch that he had followed the institute’s prescribed guidelines and procedures while dealing with student Sahil Wakode, who later died by suicide in his hostel room.Also Read | IIT Bombay suicide: Prof Suryanarayana Doolla grilled for 8 hours, denies harassment allegationsDoolla, who was sent on leave by IIT Bombay following widespread student protests, was questioned for around eight to 10 hours on the institute’s Powai campus on Friday.During his statement, Doolla told the Crime Branch that he had followed IIT Bombay’s guidelines and procedures in his handling of the events that preceded Wakode’s death.Wakode was allegedly caught using a mobile phone during a mid-semester examination on September 18. Doolla, who was invigilating the exam, asked him to leave the examination hall.The student died by suicide later that day.Doolla also denied allegations that he subjected Wakode to caste-based discrimination and mental harassment, as alleged by the student’s parents. The parents has named the professor and several others in their complaint and have demanded his arrest.Investigators are expected to examine Doolla’s statement alongside those of other people questioned in the case, as well as the evidence gathered during the probe.The Crime Branch had earlier taken over the investigation from Powai Police and has been examining digital and other evidence as part of the probe. Investigators have also questioned students, faculty members and staff connected to the case.The investigation remains underway.(With ANI inputs)Get the latest India News and Live updates. articles.summary: AMRITSAR: A woman allegedly assaulted a nearly five-year-old girl in the middle of a road in the Dharampura area of Joda Phatak on Thursday evening, with
articles.body: AMRITSAR: A woman allegedly assaulted a nearly five-year-old girl in the middle of a road in the Dharampura area of Joda Phatak on Thursday evening, with CCTV footage showing her repeatedly slapping the child, throwing her to the ground and dragging her towards her house.The incident took place around 7pm, according to the girl's family.In the CCTV footage, the girl is seen running along the road with her mother following her when the woman, identified as Anmol alias Boni, runs towards the child, grabs her and repeatedly slaps her.She then throws the girl to the ground and drags her towards her house as the child struggles to free herself.The girl's mother reaches the spot and tries to intervene, but the woman allegedly abuses and threatens her. The mother is seen falling on the road while trying to move away.Local residents then reach the spot and pull the girl away from the woman. The footage also shows the woman attempting to approach the child again before residents take her away.The child, Amania, is reported to have a problem with her legs and wears special footwear. Her father, Pankaj, told media persons that the girl had gone out to fetch some household items when the woman allegedly attacked her.He said the family was not aware of what had triggered the assault.Pankaj said a tuition teacher who reached the spot helped rescue the child, while other residents also intervened. articles.title: 'God made Trump': Inside White House's $20 million ad campaign ahead of midterms
articles.summary: The Trump administration has produced at least 13 campaign-style advertisements as part of a multimillion-dollar effort funded by US taxpayers to promote
articles.body: The Trump administration has produced at least 13 campaign-style advertisements as part of a multimillion-dollar effort funded by US taxpayers to promote President Donald Trump and his policies ahead of midterm votings.Several of the ads have not yet aired. They include three focused on the US military and operations in Iran and Venezuela, one titled “God Made Trump” and another featuring Trump's UFC event at the White House.The spending has drawn criticism from both Republicans and Democrats, who have questioned whether taxpayer money should be used for such advertising. The White House has defended the campaign by describing the videos as public service announcements.CNN obtained clips of 12 ads, ranging from 15 seconds to three minutes. Two of those had already been broadcast. The clips were stored in a Dropbox account run by LMD, the agency awarded the government contract for the advertising campaign, and were shared with CNN. Each video ends with the words “Paid for by the US Government”.Ads feature Trump's patriotic imageThree of the advertisements have so far appeared on television networks including CBS, CNN, MS NOW, Fox News and Fox. It remains unclear whether every advertisement will be broadcast on television, released digitally or both.Although the videos have different themes, many feature Trump alongside audio containing favourable comments about him from news reports. They also use patriotic imagery, including military graduation ceremonies, fireworks over Mount Rushmore and military aircraft flyovers.First lady Melania Trump appears in several of the advertisements. Other footage includes Trump's announcement of reciprocal tariffs, the US-Mexico border wall, his 2015 presidential campaign launch and a framed image depicting former President Joe Biden's autopen signature on Trump's “Presidential Walk of Fame”.CNN previously reported that Trump has personally influenced the production of the videos, including helping choose some of the footage and images, according to a source familiar with the matter.Two Trump advisers familiar with the project said the ads were being produced internally by the White House video team, which is part of the communications operation responsible for the administration's public messaging. At least one of the videos, however, was produced by a pro-Trump meme group.Spending draws bipartisan criticismThe advertisements that have already aired have faced criticism, while the White House has indicated that it intends to expand the effort.Democratic Rep. Jamie Raskin, the ranking member of the House Judiciary Committee, said in a post on X that the ads “may be felony criminal theft and conversion of government property for political campaign purposes.” If Democrats take control of the House next year, Raskin would gain congressional subpoena power. The campaign has also attracted criticism from Republicans.“Look, if you want to spend money out of your super PAC or other campaign account to communicate that message, that’s fine. It’s not an appropriate PSA. It’s just not, you know, it’s not how we should be spending taxpayer dollars,” said Sen. Thom Tillis of North Carolina.Sen. John Cornyn of Texas has also said “no” when asked whether the advertisements are an appropriate use of taxpayer money. “It’s not even a close question.”$20 million allocated for the campaignA total of $20 million has been allocated for the advertising effort, according to two sources familiar with the matter who spoke to CNN. The money is coming from Customs and Border Protection.Watchdog organisations have argued that the campaign violates appropriations laws that restrict the use of federal funds for propaganda or partisan communications.However, it remains unclear whether outside organisations have the legal standing to challenge the spending in court. While criticism has come from both parties, watchdog groups said Congress has the clearest avenue for holding the administration accountable, but lawmakers have not taken action to stop the advertisements.The White House did not directly address CNN's questions on Friday afternoon and instead pointed to a newly posted video compilation in which Trump criticised CNN.You use AI every day.
